summary: Artesunate is a water-soluble artemisinin derivative and the first-line treatment for severe malaria, given intravenously. It rapidly reduces parasite burden across all asexual stages of Plasmodium. After completing IV therapy and clinical improvement, patients must receive a full course of a follow-on oral antimalarial. A characteristic adverse effect is post-artemisinin delayed hemolysis, requiring hemoglobin monitoring for about 4 weeks after treatment.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (and severe disease from other Plasmodium species)

moa: Artesunate is a sesquiterpene lactone bearing an endoperoxide bridge. Within parasitized erythrocytes, iron (notably from heme) cleaves the endoperoxide to generate carbon-centered free radicals and reactive intermediates that alkylate and damage parasite proteins and membranes. This produces rapid, broad activity against the asexual blood stages of Plasmodium, giving the fastest parasite clearance of available antimalarials.

absolute: Known serious hypersensitivity (e.g. anaphylaxis) to artesunate
relative: Pre-existing severe anemia (monitor closely for delayed hemolysis)
monitor: Pregnancy (especially first trimester - use when benefit outweighs risk)

preg: Severe malaria in pregnancy is life-threatening to mother and fetus. WHO recommends parenteral artesunate for severe malaria in all trimesters because the benefit of prompt effective treatment outweighs potential risks; do not withhold treatment for severe disease.
lact: Breastfeeding may generally continue during treatment for severe malaria; the benefit of treating the mother and of breastfeeding is considered to outweigh potential risks given limited transfer.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is established for renal impairment; artesunate and its active metabolite dihydroartemisinin have short half-lives. Severe malaria itself may cause acute kidney injury - provide supportive care and monitor.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is established for hepatic impairment. Monitor liver function as severe malaria can cause hepatic dysfunction.

major: No major contraindicated drug interactions established for short-course parenteral artesunate
moderate: Strong CYP3A4/CYP2A6 inducers or inhibitors - may alter dihydroartemisinin exposure
Other QT-prolonging follow-on antimalarials (e.g. some ACT partner drugs) - monitor when sequenced
minor: Drugs causing hemolysis or myelosuppression - may compound anemia
interactions.diagnostics: Causes a fall in hemoglobin/reticulocyte changes from delayed hemolysis; monitor blood counts.

serious: Post-artemisinin delayed hemolysis (1-4 weeks after treatment)
rare: Acute renal failure secondary to hemolysis
emergency: Severe symptomatic delayed hemolysis requiring transfusion

monitoring: Hemoglobin and reticulocyte count during treatment and weekly for about 4 weeks after therapy to detect post-artemisinin delayed hemolysis
Renal and hepatic function and overall clinical status of severe malaria

counsel: You will receive injections in hospital followed by a full course of oral antimalarial tablets - complete the oral course
Return for blood tests for about 4 weeks; delayed anemia can occur after treatment

pk: Immediate (IV); active metabolite DHA peaks within ~25 min
Short; requires repeated dosing then oral follow-on

pearls: First-line for severe malaria - superior survival versus quinine (WHO).
Always complete a full oral antimalarial course after IV therapy to prevent recrudescence
Post-artemisinin delayed hemolysis: check hemoglobin weekly for ~4 weeks after treatment
Rapidly cleared, so requires a partner/follow-on drug for durable cure
missed: Parenteral artesunate is administered on a fixed inpatient schedule (0, 12, 24 hours then daily); a delayed dose should be given as soon as recognized and the schedule resumed. Do not omit the required follow-on oral antimalarial course.
overdose: There is limited overdose experience. Excessive dosing may increase the risk of hemolysis, neutropenia and neurologic effects. Manage supportively with monitoring of blood counts, renal function and cardiac rhythm; transfuse for severe anemia as needed.
